approachQuestion.prompt: Return the greatest common divisor of integers a and b. Both cannot be zero. The identity gcd(a,b)=gcd(b,a mod b) holds when b>0, and gcd(a,0)=a. Examples: (48,18) returns 6; (0,9) returns 9; (7,0) returns 7. Choose the method that avoids unnecessary retained state.
constraints: 0 ≤ a,b ≤ 10^18; at least one is positive. Values fit fixed-width integer words.
Remainder, assignment, and comparisons take constant time. No tail-call optimization is provided.
Return one integer. A table of results for possible inputs is not available.

options.text: While b is nonzero, replace (a,b) simultaneously with (b,a mod b); when b is zero return a.
options.feedback: The transition preserves the gcd, strictly reduces the second argument after each step, and needs only the current pair.

options.text: Return a at b=0; otherwise recursively return gcd(b,a mod b), keeping normal call frames.
options.feedback: It is correct, but all pending calls merely forward one result, so their storage can be removed with the loop.

options.text: When b is zero return zero instead of a; otherwise use the same remainder transition.
Replace (a,b) with (a mod b,b) repeatedly while b is nonzero.
options.feedback: For (48,18), this reaches (12,18) and repeats it forever instead of reducing b.

feedback.reason: Remainder preserves common divisors: gcd(a,b)=gcd(b,a mod b).
details: Keep two integer variables a and b. While b is positive, compute r=a mod b and assign a=b, b=r. Return a when b becomes zero. No recursive calls or history of earlier pairs is retained.
Remainder preserves common divisors: gcd(a,b)=gcd(b,a mod b). When b reaches zero, a is the answer. Iteration keeps constant state instead of retaining recursive remainder-call history.

“While b is nonzero, replace (a,b) simultaneously with (b,a mod b); when b is zero return a.”: The transition preserves the gcd, strictly reduces the second argument after each step, and needs only the current pair.

“Return a at b=0; otherwise recursively return gcd(b,a mod b), keeping normal call frames.”: It is correct, but all pending calls merely forward one result, so their storage can be removed with the loop.
“When b is zero return zero instead of a; otherwise use the same remainder transition.”: gcd(7,0) must be 7, not zero.
“Replace (a,b) with (a mod b,b) repeatedly while b is nonzero.”: For (48,18), this reaches (12,18) and repeats it forever instead of reducing b.

complexityQuestion.prompt: Analyze method-1 as described in the revealed method. Let M=max(2,min(a,b)) for the original inputs. Count fixed-width arithmetic as constant time. Include all temporary variables, exclude input words and returned word. No hashing or recursion is used. Choose the tightest worst-case time and auxiliary-space pair among the options.

options.text: O(log M) time, O(1) auxiliary space
O(log M) time, O(log M) auxiliary space

feedback.reason: Euclidean remainders shrink within every two steps, giving logarithmic iteration count.
details: Euclidean remainder steps shrink the smaller positive argument by a constant factor within every two steps, and consecutive Fibonacci inputs realize logarithmically many steps. A fixed number of words is retained.
“O(M) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: The remainder transition does not count down one unit at a time; the worst number of steps grows logarithmically.
“O(log M) time, O(log M) auxiliary space”: This target uses a loop, so it retains no recursive call chain.
“O(1) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: Consecutive Fibonacci-sized inputs require an increasing number of remainder steps.
